content: The following are professional interpretations of the provided references: 1. The pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and pharmacogenetics of a 400 mg daily dose of efavirenz during pregnancy and postpartum were studied, revealing critical insights into its safety and efficacy in these populations (Clin Infect Dis, 2018; 67:785–90). 2. Research has identified a potential association between dolutegravir use at conception and an increased risk of neural tube defects, emphasizing the need for careful consideration in women of childbearing potential (N Engl J Med, 2018; 379:979–81). 3. A systematic review and meta-analysis highlighted a concerning rise in pre-treatment HIV drug resistance among children in sub-Saharan Africa, underscoring the urgency of addressing this issue (J Antimicrob Chemother, 2016; 72:365–71). 4. A global collaborative framework has been proposed to accelerate the development and introduction of pediatric drug formulations for children living with HIV, addressing a critical gap in treatment accessibility (Lancet HIV, 2018; 5:e259–64). 5. The pharmacokinetics and safety of dolutegravir in pregnant women and their neonates were evaluated in the DOLPHIN-1 study, providing valuable data for its use during pregnancy (PLoS Med, 2019; 16:e1002895). 6. A modeling study assessed the risks and benefits of dolutegravirand efavirenz-based regimens for South African women with HIV of childbearing potential, offering guidance for treatment decisions (Ann Intern Med, 2019; 170:614–25). 7. The ODYSSEY trial demonstrated the safety and efficacy of simplified dolutegravir dosing in children weighing 20 kg or more, supporting its use in pediatric populations (Lancet HIV, 2020; 7(8):e533–44). 8. A systematic review and meta-analysis of dolutegravir for 7,340 patients across 13 randomized trials confirmed its efficacy and safety, even in the context of current HIV RNA suppression (Lancet Infect Dis, 2018; 18:346–55). 9. The GEMINI-1 and GEMINI-2 trials showed that dolutegravir plus lamivudine is non-inferior to a three-drug regimen in treatment-naïve adults with HIV-1, offering a simpler treatment option (Lancet, 2019; 393:143–55). 10. The FLAMINGO study compared once-daily dolutegravir with darunavir plus ritonavir in treatment-naïve adults, demonstrating the superior efficacy of dolutegravir at 48 weeks (Lancet, 2014; 383:2222–31). 11. A study on the pharmacokinetics of tenofovir alafenamide with and without cobicistat during pregnancy provided critical data for its use in this population (AIDS, 2021; 35:407–17). 12. The NADIA trial evaluated nucleosides and darunavir/dolutegravir in Africa, providing 48-week outcomes that inform second-line treatment strategies (abstract accessed June 1, 2021). 13. A meta-analysis of raltegravir-based salvage therapy over four years demonstrated its efficacy and safety in treatment-experienced patients with drug-resistant HIV-1 (Int J Antimicrob Agents, 2014; 43:189–94). 14. The ARROW trial assessed routine versus clinically driven laboratory monitoring in African children on first-line antiretroviral therapy, providing five-year outcomes to guide monitoring strategies (Lancet, 2013; 381:1391–403). 15. The GEMINI trials confirmed the efficacy of dolutegravir plus lamivudine as a two-drug regimen for treatment-naïve adults, simplifying HIV treatment while maintaining effectiveness (Lancet, 2019; 393:143–55). 16. The DAWNING study demonstrated the effectiveness of dolutegravir versus lopinavir/ritonavir in second-line therapy, with outcomes stratified by WHO-recommended NRTI backbones (abstract accessed June 1, 2021). 17. A study on dolutegravir in breast milk and maternal and infant plasma during breastfeeding provided essential safety data for its use in lactating women (AIDS, 2016; 30:2731–3). 18. The VIKING-3 study evaluated dolutegravir in patients with resistance to raltegravir and/or elvitegravir, showing promising 24-week results for this population (J Infect Dis, 2014; 210:354–62). 19. A systematic review of secondand third-line antiretroviral therapy for children and adolescents highlighted the challenges and gaps in treatment options for these populations (Pediatr Infect Dis J, 2017; 36:492–9). 20. The ACTG OPTIONS study demonstrated that omitting NRTIs from antiretroviral regimens is not inferior to adding them in treatment-experienced patients failing a protease inhibitor regimen (abstract accessed June 1, 2021). These studies collectively provide a comprehensive understanding of the efficacy, safety, and pharmacokinetics of various antiretroviral therapies across diverse populations, including pregnant women, children, and treatment-experienced patients.
